searchText: That's possible, but the risk I worry about is if there's a chain split due to a bug in an EE that we wind up with a huge number of validators suddenly being exited at once. If the client has <50% share the chain would still resolve to the valid fork fine but we could wind up exiting a huge number of validators which then potentially pushes other clients up into supermajority territory which could make things worse. I was hoping we could just have a small penalty for each invalid block but actually it would likely have to be reasonably large because a) hitting an chain split is rare and b) only the first block in the fork is likely to be eligible to penalize as the others would have an unknown parent and trying to prove that some earlier block in the chain may get expensive. Which probably means I really haven't thought this all through enough to really know what I'm talking about. 🙂 It feels like exiting the broken clients is the right thing to do here? That gets us back to finality quickly, and they can rejoin afterwards? Exiting them may actually delay finality. If it's like slashing their attestations would be ignored immediately but they'd still be assigned to committees until they get through the exit queue. Whereas if its a client with <50% share they'd just switch back to the valid chain and we likely wouldn't lose finality at all. I guess it depends on whether the bug is in most/every block or few/one block. >50% share and the broken clients would go off following their invalid chain and be hit with quadratic leak penalties on the valid chain. >67% and the invalid chain justifies and then they're stuck over there and will have to exit, get slashed for surround vote or leak out. And whether the bug allows them to still follow the correct chain or permanently splits them off. Yeah true - rejecting a valid block incorrectly would mean they'd only come back to the valid chain once they were updated with a fix. Accepting an invalid block would be less of a problem. In principle there is difference between (1) and the rest, (2) and (3) are indistinguishable. I am not sure if there is practical solution to distinguish (1) from the rest -- this is a problem I haven't thought much about, finding a solution to this problem seems at least challenging to me. Slashing for attesting to invalid block has a trade-off. It allows for punishing adversary but it also opens a way to punish honest validator driven by failing software. IMO, software that follows the protocol should protect from such an attack by rejecting invalid blocks produced and attested by adversary. I don't think buggy software should be a valid excuse for attacking the network. We already assert that if buggy software results in signing two competing blocks at the same height then you get slashed. We *should* try to limit the ways in which someone can accidentally get punished as much as possible, but if there is an attack vector I think financial punishment should always be on the table. you can also adjust the size of the punishment depending on how bad the attack is if network is very healthy and one node is behaving badly, it probably is not that big of a deal The difference is that signing two competing forks is a step towards finalizing two competing checkpoints, whereas signing off on invalid block is easy to overcome by honest actors IIUC, the attack with signing invalid blocks is that you can get finality of an invalid chain. If this chain is invalid from honest actors' view they won't follow it While if conflicting checkpoint is finalized there is no way to distinguish between honest and malicious chain But if it finalizes, someone doing a checkpoint sync or fastforward may end up following it. If adversary has enough power to force a node pulling wrong checkpoint there is no need to finalize invalid chain this can also happen onchain protocols where you want to prove that some block was finalized and have certain properties cross chain bridges come to my mind first I meant no need for attacker to do this. As other attack vectors are opening in this case, like forcing everyone to start with a conflicting finalized checkpoint IMO, slashing should only be applied for actions that are pushing a system towards a state when fully synced honest node can't decouple honest and malicious chains. Following this logic, having a penalty instead of slashing for not executing a block before attesting to it sounds reasonable. But this worth more thinking of course I think there is often confusion with the word "slashing". I think many of us use it to just mean "decreasing the person's stake" while others use it to mean a very specific type of punishment that involves an incredibly precise algorithm. Yes, I can often see this as a source of confusion here and there yeah, I think its bad terminology "double signing" could be better Slashing is a specific penalty for "double signing" yeah, I was recommending to stop using "slashing" I agree, we should stop using outside of the double signing context, at least for now (probably in the future we will slash for some other actions as well) well for me outside of the core development, "slashing" sounds like it would mean any kind of punishment Yeah, I was going to recommend not using slashing to refer to such a specific thing. 😄 Yes, I can understand that but "slashing" is a term that people will have to learn has a special meaning because it is in the foundation of the protocol It is a pretty generic term to mean "cutting someone" (or in this case, cutting their money). Eth2.0 used to be too, and we have gotten rid of it quite nicely too :) I will admit, there *is* value in having *some* term for each of the specific penalties. Inactivity leaking penalty, slashing penalty, etc. 🤔 Inactivity leaking is quite easy to understand slashing could be just "double signing" which is also again more understandable I think part of the problem is that "slashing" it used by other blockchains to mean some other kind of "reduce stake of staker". While inactivity leak is quite specific and not used in conflicting ways outside of Ethereum. I like "double signing penalty". It is much more specific. "nothing at stake penalty" could also be one idea. But maybe too far fetched Hello, I joined goerli testnet 2.0 merge, but I found all method return "method eth_getFilterChanges does not exist/is not available", any pointer to solve this is highly appreciated. could you please stop spamming the same message on multiple channels Sorry, Please ignore it. "slashing condition" is the term used by the Casper FFG paper. As for me it is more fundamental than the Eth2.0 was the feature is fundamental, not the name of it "A slashing condition" is fine I think, but we should have a name for that condition that is specific (double signing). The idea is that there can be many conditions that lead to slashing. A slashable offense would be another valid phrase I think, and it would be less specific than "A double signing offense". this just get shottened to slashing easily Right, but I think in that context it is a generic term. "A slashing condition" vs "The slashing condition". ~~https://blockchainisaconcretecountablenoun.com/~~ https://slashingisaconcretecountablenoun.com/ (I will not defend this claim) The problem with this situation is that exactly the opposite is the most likely to happen: in case of a bug in a EE client, we'd see lots of people being slashed and according to your rule they'll end up with a higher penalty. I agree that it's a subtle issue trying to decide if we slash for behavior that may end up being due to a client bug, but if this behavior is indistinguishable from a coordinated attack, then we need to decide priorities. right, it doesnt work for every bug but works on individual level quite nicely if the bug is in ones specific setup
